fields.title: RTO and RPO Explained Simply
fields.keyTakeaway: RPO determines how much data we lose, RTO determines how fast we return, and an untested backup is not a backup.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: The database is corrupted. Two questions determine everything else: how long to recover and what do we lose?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: These two numbers determine the backup architecture and its cost. If not defined in advance, they are determined by chance — how an engineer set up backups three years ago. And they surface the moment data is already lost.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: **[[rto|RTO]]** — how fast we must restore operations. An hour, four hours, a day.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **[[rpo|RPO]]** — how much data is acceptable to lose. Determined by backup frequency: a daily backup means losing up to a day of work.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: These are different things, and confusing them is costly. You can recover in 15 minutes while losing a day's worth of data. You can lose nothing yet take six hours to recover.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: The product way to set these numbers is to ask: **how much data are we ready to ask users to re-enter, and how long can we be down without losing them?**
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: Separately: RPO and RTO differ for different data. Losing an hour of analytics is nothing. Losing an hour of orders is a catastrophe.
fields.sections/2/blocks/8/text: The main practical rule: **a backup that has never been restored from is not a backup.** [[restore-drill|Restore drills]] once a quarter regularly reveal that backups are incomplete, corrupted, or take ten times longer to restore than expected.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: The catalog is an interesting case: formally the data is important, but it is restored from the source, so RPO is soft. The right question is not "how important is the data" but "where do we get it if we lose it."
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: First restore drill: the claimed 1 hour turned into 4 hours 20 minutes. The reason — the procedure was written down but not tested, and restoring the primary database required manual steps known to only one person. After two iterations, they met the 50-minute target.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Data recovery is not equal to operational recovery: the database is back, but services need restarting, caches warmed up, queues cleared. RTO is measured until the user can work, not when the database comes up.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: RPO determines how much data we lose, RTO determines how fast we return, and an untested backup is not a backup.
